claims.text: Short-range chemical ordering governs the high-temperature structural stability of near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles.
Robust nanoparticle-support interactions govern high-temperature structural stability by reducing coarsening.
Short-range ordering and robust support interactions reduce phase segregation in low-noble-metal, near-equiatomic nanoparticles.
Precursor mixing and thermal processing can be used to vary short-range chemical order.
Changing carbon-substrate defect density changes nanoparticle interfacial anchoring.
Short-range chemical order can change rapidly over a narrow temperature interval and accompany phase transformation.
Enhanced short-range ordering lowers the thermodynamic driving force for phase segregation.
Enhanced short-range ordering lowers the thermodynamic driving force for sintering.
Defective turbostratic graphite provides nanoparticle nucleation and anchoring sites.
Partial intercalation and rooting at graphite edge planes produce high nanoparticle-support binding energy.
Strong anchoring at defective carbon sites inhibits morphological transformation and improves thermal stability.
Strong interfacial interactions maintain a near-equiatomic compositional distribution during extended high-temperature exposure.
Particles with stronger carbon-support interactions will coarsen less than particles with weaker support bonding under identical thermal and reactive conditions.
Particles with greater short-range ordering will coarsen less and undergo less compositional drift than less-ordered particles.
Particles deposited on smoother, lower-defect supports will exhibit faster grain growth than those on defective carbon supports.
Less-ordered particles will exhibit faster surface segregation under identical thermal and reactive conditions.
Carbon-supported nanoparticles can retain excellent thermal stability during in situ annealing up to 1173 K.
The proposed mechanism is most pronounced for near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles at 773–1173 K.
Substantially higher temperatures, higher noble-metal content, or heavy doping may change the interplay between ordering and interfacial effects.
Rapid quenching or intentional doping can diminish or frustrate short-range ordering.
